## What this pack is steering

The rep's words: *"claims ops people at mid-sized UK insurers who are drowning in complaints"*. Direct motion, GB, 20 firms wanted, three weeks, email and LinkedIn only.

The spine of the argument is a coverage gap with a regulatory consequence. Claims and complaint handling in UK general insurance is overwhelmingly a telephone process, and quality assurance on that telephony is done by human sampling — a QA analyst listens to a handful of calls per agent per month. The facts file's live capability is that every call the pipeline ingests is transcribed and scored against the customer's own QA rules (i360.product.every-ingested-call-analysed, i360.feature.auto-qa-scoring-against-tenant-rules). That is the displacement: sampled human QA out, scored-on-ingest QA in. The complaint angle is the wedge because complaints are the one place where the unreviewed call becomes a cost — a Financial Ombudsman case fee, an uphold, a remediation exercise.

**Ready now.** Everything in the wedge is shipped: scoring against tenant rules, configurable risk types that flag vulnerability-related calls (the facts file's REFRAME wording — never call it a vulnerability-detection module), the calls explorer with filters, per-call detail with transcript, summary and coaching points, the agents pages, the needs-review list, and the append-only settings audit log. Pricing is public and confirmed: GBP 4.99 / 7.99 / 9.99 per seat per month with pooled hours, GBP 0.50 per hour overage, GBP 1,280 setup and GBP 640 config review, no seat minimum, no annual lock-in.

**What must not lead.** Three of the most tempting insurance angles are boundaries, not capabilities. There are no regulator-ready evidence packs (an FCA Consumer Duty pack is explicitly `planned`). There is no in-app audio playback, so "listen to the evidence" is out. There is no group or cross-tenant dashboard, which matters because insurance groups and consolidated brokers will ask for it. There is no PII or card redaction and no SSO/SCIM — a regulated buyer's security review will ask, and the honest answer is no. The product is post-call only and does not record calls; it analyses recordings the customer's own telephony already makes. Results land within a couple of hours, not minutes. Hosting is EU (Frankfurt), not UK — the wiki's "never leaves UK" line is wrong and must never be repeated to a UK insurer, who will check.

**Telephony reality.** Automated feeds exist for 3CX, OAK/ClarifyGo and RingCentral (RingCX and RingEX; the RingCentral fact overrides the knowledge set's older articles). Everything else — Teams, Cisco, Avaya, Mitel, 8x8, Five9 — is "works with recordings from", scoped per customer. Mid-sized UK insurers skew to Teams, Avaya and Genesys-class estates; assume a scoping conversation, not a turn-key connector, and treat that as a qualifying question rather than a claim.

**Hard filters, derived.** Geography is Great Britain: England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland is not GB and firms headquartered there are out of this brief's region even where the FCA regulates them. Size is bounded by the product's own ICP band of 5 to 250 contact-centre seats, so "mid-sized" here means an insurance operation with a contact centre inside that band — which in practice means MGAs, specialist personal-lines insurers, claims-handling TPAs and mid-tier brokers, not the composite majors whose claims floors run into thousands of seats. Firms already on a full CCaaS with an embedded QM module they cannot unbundle are still in scope as a displacement conversation, but firms wanting real-time agent assist, pure MiFID-style voice retention, or marketing call attribution are out of category.

**Prior packs.** None exist for this product in this org, so nothing in this pack is inherited and m14 has no prior claims to reconcile.

**Hypotheses to test in the waves below** (not findings): that Financial Ombudsman case-fee exposure is a sharper trigger than Consumer Duty for a claims ops buyer; that claims-handling TPAs feel the pain harder than insurers because they are judged on their client's complaint numbers; that the vulnerability/Consumer Duty outcomes-monitoring requirement is what makes a 2–5% sample indefensible in writing.

m01.body:
## The shape of the market this brief points at

The rep asked for "claims ops people at mid-sized UK insurers who are drowning in complaints". That phrase describes a real and currently moving market, but the boundary of it is not the one the phrase implies. Complaint volume in UK general insurance is concentrated in a handful of product lines, and the operations that handle those complaints are frequently *not* inside the carrier. They sit in third-party administrators, in MGAs with delegated claims authority, in assistance and repair-network operators, and in the outsourced arms of consolidated brokers. The FCA has said as plainly as it says anything that outsourcing does not displace accountability, and that it is expanding its review of "how firms oversee third parties that handle claims". That single sentence is why the buyer set for this campaign is wider than "insurer" and why every seat inside the 5-250 band that touches a policyholder on the phone about a claim is in scope.

Three forces are pushing at once, and all three are dated inside the last twelve months. First, the regulator moved from thematic review to action: on 18 December 2025 the FCA published its response to the Which? super-complaint and confirmed two enforcement cases opened, one firm stopped from growing its business, three independent reviews into firms' systems and controls, and three senior managers made to agree fixes. Second, the cost of a complaint that escapes went up: from 1 April 2026 the Financial Ombudsman charges respondent firms GBP 680 per case, with a GBP 2,000 annual free allowance replacing the old three-free-cases arrangement. Third, the volume in the two lines the FCA is looking hardest at is rising, not falling: FOS Q1 2026/27 data shows car or motorcycle insurance complaints up to 4,100 from 2,800 a year earlier and travel insurance up 30% to 1,300.

The operational consequence, and this is the seam the product sits in, is evidential rather than emotional. Under PRIN 2A the firm is judged on outcomes it can demonstrate, and the FCA's own commentary is that firms struggle to turn management information into actionable insight. A claims operation that samples 2-5% of its calls has management information about 2-5% of its calls. That is the gap. It is worth noting as an inference, not a finding, that this is why complaint root-cause analysis keeps appearing in FCA good-practice publications as an area for improvement: the raw material for root-cause work on telephone claims journeys mostly does not exist in a form anyone can query.

The counter-current is real and the campaign agent should hold it. Coverage is no longer a novel selling point in this market. MaxContact's 2026 research with 285 FCA-regulated UK contact centre managers and directors found manual sampling and AI reviewing every call running almost neck and neck at 49.5% and 46.7%. If that sample is representative of regulated contact centres generally, roughly half the addressable set will answer "we already have that" to a coverage-led opener. The same research found 54.0% had found a compliance breach or harm issue outside their routine QA sample, which is the more interesting fact and the more defensible opener: the problem has moved from *how much you review* to *what you can prove and how fast anything changes as a result*.

On size: the ceiling matters more than the floor here. A composite motor insurer's claims floor runs well past 250 seats and is out of the band by product design. What is inside the band is the specialist end — a travel insurer's claims and assistance desk, an MGA's delegated claims team, a TPA's motor FNOL operation, a pet or home-emergency claims unit, a broker consolidator's central complaints function. Those are the sub-segments below, and the fit verdicts follow the complaint density in the FOS and FCA data rather than the prestige of the brand.

m02.body:
## Who else is in the room

The competitive set for this brief is not the enterprise workforce-optimisation suites. It is three narrower things: the mid-market auto-QA platforms that publish per-user prices and are actively marketing at UK regulated contact centres; the UK conversation-analytics vendors that have built their entire pitch on FCA conduct risk and vulnerable customers; and the status quo, which is a person listening to four to eight calls per handler a month and filling in a form.

**EvaluAgent is the reference point on price and on packaging.** It is UK-headquartered, publishes rates openly - from USD 35 per user per month for AutoQM and from USD 65 with the conversation-intelligence bundle - and its feature comparison table names, item by item, the things a regulated insurance buyer will ask about: SSO and MFA on all plans, PII redaction and entity recognition, custom redaction rules, audit log, SOC 2 Type II, EU and US data residency options, and listening back to the recording alongside the transcript. That list matters more than the price. Insights360's facts file marks SSO, SCIM, PII redaction and listening to recordings inside the application as not shipped; what it provides per call is the transcript, the per-rule scores, the summary, the risk flags and the coaching points. Against this competitor, a features bake-off on security and evidence surfaces is a losing frame; the winning frame is the one the facts file supports - price accessible below a QA function's economic floor, no seat minimum, no annual commitment.

**Scorebuddy is the opaque one.** Three quote-based tiers, per-user licence plus metered AI scoring credits (500 a month on Accelerate, 1,000 on Elite), and third-party listings that put a floor somewhere around USD 24 per month. Its claim of more than 300 organisations in 25+ countries and its published customer quotes are its proof; its weakness is that a small MGA cannot find out what it costs without a sales call. Openly published per-seat pricing is the sharpest available contrast, and the brand voice explicitly permits quoting prices - though outbound rules keep price to the offer stage and forbid naming any rival.

**The UK conduct-risk specialists are the real threat to the wedge.** MaxContact has published research with 285 FCA-regulated UK contact centres and is using it to own the exact anxiety this campaign is built on - its own site-wide banner leads with "54% of FCA-regulated contact centres missed a breach". Voyc and Aveni sell vulnerability identification directly against the FCA's vulnerable-customers framework, with Aveni Detect listed on the Genesys AppFoundry. These vendors are not necessarily better products, but they have arrived first at the same door with the same regulatory story, and at least one of them is already inside the CCaaS marketplaces that mid-sized insurers buy from. The facts file's own guidance is decisive here: Insights360 has configurable risk types that flag vulnerability-related calls, and it is not a purpose-built vulnerability-detection module. One inference worth stating plainly, drawn from reading these vendors' own pages rather than from any single claim: the vulnerability story is now crowded at the top of the funnel and thin at the bottom, because none of these specialists publishes a price. That is the gap the pricing table below exploits.

**The do-nothing option is strong and must be respected.** Manual sampling satisfies most client contracts and most internal policies today, and the FCA's direction of travel in 2026 is deregulatory in tone: CP26/22, published 29 June 2026, proposes stripping overlapping and outdated requirements from the insurance rulebook, and Clifford Chance reports the FCA has confirmed firms do not need to produce a standalone Consumer Duty board report. A claims director can reasonably read the year as one in which the paperwork burden is falling, not rising. The counter is not regulatory fear - it is the Ombudsman's case fee, which went up to GBP 680 per case on 1 April 2026 regardless of how the rulebook is simplified.

m03.body:
## Four situations, not four job titles

The rep's phrase - "claims ops people at mid-sized UK insurers" - describes a role, and roles do not buy. Situations buy. The four below are the situations in UK general insurance where a claims telephone operation of between roughly 20 and 250 seats is under enough pressure, from a named source, to change how it reviews its calls. They differ in who owns the pain, who signs, and what the sale is actually about.

The first, **the outsourced claims handler**, is the sharpest because its pain is commercial as well as regulatory. When the FCA says it will improve claims handling by reviewing firms' customer service and delivery and how they oversee third parties that handle claims, the immediate operational consequence lands on the third party: their carrier client now needs evidence about the handler's phone calls, and the handler is the only party who can produce it. Their client-service reviews already run on quality scores, and quality assurance scoring is one of the key call centre metrics by which handling is measured; the difference is that the client now needs those scores to cover more than a review sample. This is the one situation where the buyer can plausibly charge the value onward - an inference from the contract structure, not a sourced claim.

The second, **the travel and assistance claims desk**, is the one the regulator is looking directly at. Travel insurance complaints rose 30% year on year to 1,300 cases in April to June 2026 and the most common complaint issue was declined claims; the Ombudsman itself told a House of Lords committee that in some cases travel claim outcomes are determined by agents of the insurer rather than the insurer, and that declined claims account for around 56% of travel complaints. Small teams, seasonal peaks, high emotional load, and every declined-claim conversation a potential case fee.

The third, **the delegated-authority MGA**, is the smallest and the fastest. An MGA works under a Binding Authority and is subject to ongoing oversight and regular audits by its carrier partners and their investors, while running a lean permanent team that is not required to maintain as many specified roles as an insurance company. It is inside the seat band by construction, has no enterprise QA tooling and often no QA analyst at all, and can decide in one meeting. The trade-off is deal size: at 15 seats the annual licence is small money, and the GBP 1,280 setup fee is a larger share of year one than it is anywhere else.

The fourth, **the specialist motor claims operation**, has the most volume and the most complaints. Car and motorcycle insurance complaints at the Ombudsman rose to 4,100 in April to June 2026, up from 2,800 in the same period in 2025, with consumers raising concerns about claim values, policy cancellations and claim delays. Below the composite majors sit motor carriers and insurtechs whose whole staff count is in the low hundreds - the claims and FNOL floor is the operation, and the QA function is one or two people. The pull here is coverage arithmetic; the risk is that this is the segment most likely to already have an auto-QA tool, since 46.7% of the FCA-regulated contact centres surveyed already have AI reviewing every single call.

Across all four, one structural note the campaign agent must hold. Agents are not users of this product and must not be contacted (that is a facts-file boundary, not a preference). The people who sign, champion and run it are the claims operations lead, the QA or quality lead, and the compliance or conduct-risk officer. The finance sign-off is usually the same operations director, because at published list prices this is not a capital decision - an inference from the price list, not a sourced finding. Telephony is the qualifying question in every one of these situations: automated feeds exist for 3CX, OAK/ClarifyGo and RingCentral, and everything else is a per-customer scoping conversation. In insurance specifically, expect Teams, Avaya and Genesys-class estates more often than 3CX, so treat the connector question as the first disqualifier rather than the last.

## How to find these firms, and how to throw most of them away

The hard part of this brief is not finding UK insurance firms. It is finding the ones whose claims telephone operation sits inside 5-250 seats. Published headcount is not seat count, and in insurance the gap is large: a carrier with 800 staff may run a 90-seat claims floor, and a broker with 200 staff may run none at all because claims are delegated out. Every seed below is therefore sized on the best public evidence available and labelled honestly as confirmed, estimated or unknown. Nothing here is a list; these are eleven firms a rep can check by hand to test whether the recipe produces the right shape of company.

The most valuable targeting insight in this pack is that **the Ombudsman and the FCA both publish the qualifying data for free**. The FOS half-yearly business complaints data names every firm against which it received and resolved at least a threshold number of complaints, with volumes and uphold rates; the FCA publishes firm-specific complaints returns twice a year and requires firms above its reporting thresholds to publish a summary on their own websites. A rep can therefore see a prospect's complaint exposure before making contact, and can filter by product line to hit motor, travel or property specifically. Two cautions. First, both datasets have publication thresholds, so the smallest MGAs and every TPA are invisible in them - the absence of a firm proves nothing. Second, the data names the *respondent* firm, which for delegated business is the carrier or the MGA, not the claims handler doing the talking; getting from a complaint volume to the operation that produced it takes one more step.

For the operations that never appear in complaints data - TPAs, assistance providers, outsourced claims desks - the useful discovery route is the reverse one: consumer-facing comparison and review work that names who actually handles the claim. Which?'s 2026 travel insurance review lists the claims handler alongside each policy, which is effectively a published directory of who runs travel claims desks in the UK. The MGAA's member listings do the same job for MGAs and for the suppliers that serve them.

On triggers: the strongest ones in this market are dated regulatory and financial events (a case-fee change, a published review, a results statement showing growth) rather than hiring signals. Claims job adverts are abundant but low-signal - they run continuously in this sector. Prefer a firm that has just launched a new product line into a complaint-heavy market, just won or lost a delegated authority, or just appeared in a published complaints table.

m05.body:
## What actually hurts, in order

The pains below are ordered by acuteness within each kind of buyer, and acuteness here means *how close the pain sits to a dated consequence*. A regulator's published review with enforcement attached beats a general frustration; a per-case fee with a date beats a feeling that quality could be better.

Two mechanisms run underneath almost all of them and are worth stating once. The first is the **sampling ceiling**. The industry standard for manual call QA is four to six calls per agent per month, and Call Centre Helper's own research found 41% of contact centres monitoring fewer than four. On a claims floor that is a rounding error against volume, and the practitioners quoted below say so themselves - one describes analysing over 100 calls a day single-handed for a 60-70 seat centre, another says monitoring ten calls per agent per *day* would be impossible. Whatever number a claims operation quotes, its QA coverage is a sample chosen by a person with limited time.

The second is the **evidence chain**. The FCA's complaints and root-cause review of 40 firms found the good practice was already there in the shape of established root-cause processes and clear escalation routes, and that the failures were downstream: complaints MI not granular enough to show outcomes for different groups of customers including those with characteristics of vulnerability, no clear evidence that data had been discussed at decision-making forums, and no measurement of whether interventions worked. That is a specific, published diagnosis. A claims operation whose call-level record covers 2-5% of conversations cannot make its complaints MI more granular, because the granularity does not exist.

One honest counterweight, which belongs here rather than only in the contradictions module: coverage alone no longer astonishes anyone. Roughly half of FCA-regulated contact centres report AI reviewing every call. The pain that still bites, on the same research, is that 54.0% found a compliance breach or harm issue outside their routine QA sample and the average gap between a call and the agent hearing about it is 3.08 days. The live wound is latency and provability, not volume.

claims.text: The accepted call-centre industry standard for manual QA scoring is random scoring of four advisor calls per month, and Call Centre Helper's research found 41% of contact centres monitoring fewer than four calls per advisor per month.

The FCA's thematic review of complaints and root cause analysis across 40 firms identified three areas for improvement: complaints management information not granular enough to show outcomes for different customer types including those with characteristics of vulnerability; unclear evidence that the data was discussed at decision-making forums and what actions would follow; and firms not always measuring the impact of the interventions they made.

The FCA selected the firms for its complaints and root-cause review using Financial Ombudsman uphold rates for each firm, firms' own uphold rates, the time taken to deal with complaints and total complaint volume in the last 12 months, with a baseline of at least 90 complaints to the Ombudsman in the last three years.

pains.text: The TPA's insurer clients are now inside an FCA workplan that reviews how they oversee third parties handling their claims, so the client's oversight team asks the TPA for evidence of call quality that a monthly sample of a few calls per handler cannot support. The mechanism is simple: the accountability stays with the carrier, the calls happen at the TPA, and only the TPA can produce the record.

pains.role: Contact centre industry professional, Call Centre Helper community
pains.text: In outsourced environments the number of calls monitored is set by the client contract rather than by risk, and without dedicated quality monitors the number cannot be raised - so the coverage is whatever was negotiated, not whatever the exposure requires.
pains.quote: The number of calls to monitor per agent is a debated topic within the industry. On average, I've seen 4 to 8 calls per month as a common range. However, in some cases, the quantity monitored is driven by client requirements, which can influence the number of calls reviewed.
pains.speaker: Jeff

pains.text: Over half of FCA-regulated contact centres (54.0%) have found a compliance breach or harm issue outside their routine QA sample, and for 16.5% it has happened more than once - which for an outsourcer means the discovery is often made by, or in front of, the client.

The average time between a call and the handler getting feedback on it is 3.08 days across FCA-regulated contact centres, with only 10.9% managing it inside a day; in a claims operation that is several more days of the same handling behaviour on live files before anything changes.

The FCA found that although complaints management information was captured, it was not always granular enough to tell the firm about outcomes for different groups of customers, including those with characteristics of vulnerability - a gap an outsourcer cannot close from complaint files alone, because the signal is in the conversation.

Around 56% of travel insurance complaints brought to the Financial Ombudsman relate to a declined claim, and these disputes turn on whether exclusions, limitations, eligibility and disclosure obligations were understood - which in practice means whether they were explained properly on a phone call that no one reviewed.

Travel insurance complaints to the Ombudsman rose 30% year on year to 1,300 in April-June 2026, in the same period as the FCA expanded its claims-handling work on home and travel following the Which? super-complaint - rising volume and rising scrutiny at the same time.

The Which? super-complaint specifically cited failure to identify customers in vulnerable circumstances and support them appropriately as one of the poor claims-handling practices, alongside ineffective communication about expectations, progress and outcomes - both of which are audible on the call and invisible in the claim file.

pains.text: On a small desk with seasonal peaks, the quality workload is simply not survivable at any meaningful sample rate - practitioners describe ten calls per agent per month as already the limit and ten per day as impossible because of the amount of work involved.
pains.quote: I monitor 10 calls per agent per month using a quality monitoring form. These calls often contain detailed information that needs to be verified, clarified, or followed up on. Monitoring 10 calls per agent per day in our call centre would be impossible due to the amount of work involved.
pains.speaker: Joda

pains.text: The Financial Ombudsman has told Parliament that in some cases travel claim outcomes are determined by agents of the insurer rather than the insurer itself, which puts the travel desk in the position of both being overseen and having to oversee - and the evidence for both directions is the same set of unreviewed calls.

pains.text: Insurers must evidence active oversight across managing general agents, third-party administrators and third-party networks, so the capacity provider's own regulatory obligation converts directly into audit questions for the MGA - and the MGA's claims quality evidence is whatever its claims lead happened to check.

The FCA acknowledges smaller firms may take a proportionate approach with fewer resources and simpler governance, but states that all firms have a Duty to act to deliver good outcomes - so being small removes the excuse without removing the work.

pains.text: From April 2026 the Financial Ombudsman replaced three free cases a year with a GBP 2,000 annual allowance and charges GBP 680 per case above it, so a small MGA that previously paid nothing for a handful of referrals now has a direct, countable cost attached to complaints it failed to resolve.

Mid-market QA platforms start at around USD 35 per user per month for automated scoring and USD 65 with conversation intelligence, with volume discounts aimed at larger contact centres - economics that assume a QA function an MGA claims team of a dozen people does not have.

pains.role: Insurance operations and complaints management professional (LinkedIn headline)
pains.text: In insurance and financial services complaints are routinely treated as a back-office obligation rather than as the clearest available signal about what is broken, which is why the same complaint themes persist year after year in the same places.
pains.quote: Too often, complaints management is: - Seen as back-office noise - Underinvested in - Managed for compliance, not insight. Yet complaints are one of the clearest signals we get from customers about what's broken - in our products, processes, or communication.
pains.speaker: Rav Sandhu

pains.text: Car or motorcycle insurance complaints to the Ombudsman rose to 4,100 in April-June 2026 from 2,800 a year earlier, with claim values, policy cancellations and claim delays named as the drivers - all of which are argued out on the phone before they become a complaint.

Every referred case above the GBP 2,000 annual allowance costs the firm GBP 680, and motor is about a third of all insurance cases referred to the Ombudsman - so a motor claims operation carries the largest per-firm case-fee exposure of any line in this pack.

pains.role: Contact centre industry professional, Call Centre Helper community
pains.text: A weekly monitored call per handler - four a month, the industry standard - tells you almost nothing about a handler taking 50 or more calls a day, and raising the number is limited by the quality-monitoring resource the operation can afford rather than by the risk it carries.
pains.quote: Our target is to monitor one call per agent per week... However, such targets don't always reflect the workload of individual agents. For example, monitoring one call per week doesn't provide much insight for agents handling 50 or more calls a day.
pains.speaker: Bunny

pains.text: Even with good scorecards and calibration sessions, different human evaluators interpret the same interaction differently, producing inconsistent scoring and a sense of unfairness among agents that undermines trust in the QA process itself - so the sample is not only small, it is contested.

The FCA found firms did not always measure the impact of the interventions they made after complaints analysis, meaning operations sometimes pursued actions that were not as effective as they needed to be - a failure mode that persists as long as the before-and-after evidence is a hand-picked sample.

## How these people actually talk

Three things stand out in the language and all three should change how outreach is written.

First, **claims and quality people count in calls per agent per month, not in percentages**. Vendors say "2-5% coverage"; practitioners say "four a week", "ten a month", "one per agent per week alongside a PEP session". A cold email that opens with a percentage sounds like a vendor. One that opens with "four calls per handler a month" sounds like someone who has stood on the floor. The percentage is the argument; the calls-per-month is the language.

Second, **the complaints people frame complaints as signal, not as failure**. The most articulate practitioner voice found in this market talks about complaints as "gifts in disguise", as "signals that something isn't connecting", and asks whether firms are "really improving, or just reporting". That framing is a gift for outreach because it is not defensive: it lets the message be about learning from the calls rather than about catching people out. It also warns against the opposite framing - anything that sounds like "your agents are getting it wrong" will be read as an attack on a team the reader manages and protects.

Third, **the regulator's own words are more usable than any vendor's**. "Evidence", "outcomes", "root cause", "oversight of third parties", "management information" - these are the words that appear in the documents this buyer is currently being measured against, and they are neutral, unhyped and specific. Borrow them. Avoid the vendor register entirely: no "revolutionise", no "AI-powered", no "unlock". The brand voice bans those anyway, and this audience has been marketed at by every conversation-analytics vendor in the market this year.

A note on what is thin. Buyer language specific to *insurance claims* QA - as opposed to contact-centre QA in general - is scarce in public. The insurance-side voices found are complaints and operations professionals writing about complaints handling in general, and a former claims handler quoted in vendor research. The richest first-person material about call sampling comes from the general contact-centre community, where contributors are identified by first name only. Treat those as real practitioner voices (the publication describes them as its community of industry professionals) but not as insurance-specific ones, and note the gap in m18.

phrases.notThis: Do not say "your QA is inadequate" - the sample size was not their decision and saying so insults the person who has been defending it.

phrases.say: "Improving, or just reporting?" is the sharpest single line available for this audience. It lets outreach acknowledge that the client pack already exists and still lands the point: the pack is built from a sample, so it reports on a sample.
phrases.role: Insurance operations and complaints management professional (LinkedIn headline)
phrases.text: Complaints professionals distinguish sharply between reporting on complaints and actually improving - a decade of dashboards with the same themes recurring is the specific failure they name.
phrases.quote: We've had a decade of data, dashboards, and "improvement plans." But if the same themes keep coming back... are we really improving, or just reporting?
phrases.notThis: Do not use it accusingly at a named firm. It is a question the industry asks itself, not a charge to level at a prospect.
phrases.speaker: Rav Sandhu

phrases.say: Quote the regulator, not the vendor. "The FCA said in December it is reviewing how firms oversee the third parties that handle their claims" is a fact the reader can check in thirty seconds, and it makes the email about their world rather than about a product.
phrases.role: Director of competition and interim director of insurance, FCA
phrases.text: The regulator's own framing of the work now under way names claims handling and third-party oversight as the two things being reviewed.
phrases.quote: We've set out more detail on the action we've already taken to fix problems, and we're expanding our existing workplan to improve the claims process and consumer understanding of their cover.
phrases.notThis: Never extend it into a compliance promise. The product does not produce regulator-ready evidence packs and must never be positioned as making anyone compliant.
phrases.speaker: Graeme Reynolds

phrases.say: Lead with the impossibility, not the ambition: "You are not going to review more calls by hand - there aren't the hours in the week, especially in peak season." Then offer the scoring as something that happens without anyone listening first.
phrases.role: Contact centre industry professional, Call Centre Helper community
phrases.text: Small-desk quality leads describe higher sampling not as undesirable but as arithmetically impossible given the follow-up each reviewed call generates.
phrases.quote: Monitoring 10 calls per agent per day in our call centre would be impossible due to the amount of work involved.
phrases.notThis: Avoid "listen to 100% of your calls" - it describes an activity the reader knows they cannot do and, in this product's case, is also not what happens.
phrases.speaker: Joda

phrases.say: Frame the offer around the handler's hardest conversation - the delay update and the decline - rather than around management visibility. "The calls your team dreads are the ones nobody reviews" is closer to how this desk experiences the problem.
phrases.role: Former claims handler, quoted in the Customer Experience: The Claim Handler's Perspective research report
phrases.text: Claims handlers describe the main source of stress as the customer's frustration with pace, not the technical work of the claim.
phrases.quote: The main source of stress came from dealing with frustrated customers who were unhappy with the pace at which things were progressing.
phrases.notThis: Do not frame it as agent surveillance. Agents are not users of this product and the team lead will hear monitoring language as a threat to their people.
phrases.speaker: Natalie

phrases.say: Use it to establish that the desk's calls are the deciding artefact: the outcome the Ombudsman later reviews was set in a conversation on their floor. That is a statement of fact from the Ombudsman, not a pitch.
phrases.role: Written evidence CIM0040 to the House of Lords Financial Services Regulation Committee
phrases.text: The Ombudsman's own description of travel claims puts the deciding action in the hands of the insurer's agents, which is the language a travel desk will recognise as describing itself.
phrases.quote: In some cases, claim outcomes are determined by agents of the insurer, rather than the insurer itself.
phrases.notThis: Do not imply the Ombudsman criticises the desk. The sentence explains a structure; it does not allege wrongdoing.
phrases.speaker: Financial Ombudsman Service

phrases.say: "Managed for compliance, not insight" is the phrase to mirror. For an MGA it converts a cost conversation into a product-and-process one: the same calls that satisfy the capacity provider's audit also tell you which product wording is causing the complaints.
phrases.role: Insurance operations and complaints management professional (LinkedIn headline)
phrases.text: Complaints professionals in insurance frame complaints as underinvested customer intelligence rather than as a regulatory chore - the framing a small MGA leadership team responds to, because it makes the spend about the business rather than about compliance.
phrases.quote: Too often, complaints management is: - Seen as back-office noise - Underinvested in - Managed for compliance, not insight.
phrases.notThis: Do not promise the audit outcome. Never write that this satisfies a binder audit or a Consumer Duty requirement.

## What the product actually answers

Every pain identified in m05, across all four kinds of buyer, maps to a capability the facts file marks shipped. That is a genuinely strong position for this brief: the wedge (scoring on ingest instead of on a sample) is not aspirational. But three cautions run through the table below and are worth stating once rather than twenty times.

First, several pains sit downstream of a regulatory or financial consequence - a case fee, an Ombudsman referral, a client's oversight review - that the product does not remove. Scoring and flagging every ingested call gives the operation earlier visibility into the handling patterns that precede those consequences; it does not itself reduce a case-fee bill or an uphold rate, and no case-study number exists anywhere in the sources to support such a claim. Every mapping that touches a financial or regulatory outcome carries a `mustNotImply` note saying so.

Second, three of the sharpest insurance-specific asks - a regulator-ready evidence pack, in-app audio playback of a flagged moment, and a consolidated view across an MGA's or TPA's several client entities - are marked `planned`, not `live`, in the facts file. Where a pain naturally suggests one of these, the mapping below deliberately answers with the shipped adjacent capability (the per-call PDF, the audit log, the tenant's own scoring) and names the boundary rather than implying the fuller thing.

Third, the vulnerability-flagging capability that matters most to the travel desk is configurable risk types, not a purpose-built vulnerability-detection module - the facts file's own reframing note is binding and repeated wherever the pain touches vulnerable-customer identification.

No pain from m05 is left unmatched; the table below covers all twenty.

## The buyer this campaign should actually find

The ideal company is not 'a mid-sized UK insurer' in the sense of a brand name; it is any GB claims or complaints telephone operation, wherever it sits legally, whose seat count falls inside the product's own 5-250 band. That reframing matters because the operation that answers a policyholder's call is frequently not the carrier - it is a TPA, an MGA with delegated authority, or an outsourced assistance desk - and the FCA has said plainly it is reviewing how firms oversee exactly those third parties. The ideal buyer is therefore whoever inside that operation owns how call quality is measured and has to answer, in writing, for what the operation can evidence: a claims operations or QA lead, a compliance or conduct-risk officer, or at the smallest end, the MD or COO who is both.

The disqualifiers below are stricter than 'not a fit' - several are boundaries the product cannot honestly cross today, and selling into a buyer whose decision depends on one of them sets an expectation this product will fail to meet at the security review or the second demo, which is worse for the account than never opening it.

## How to talk to each kind of buyer

The brand voice's core instruction - lead with the operational problem, quote units of work openly, name the boundary, no transformation language, short sentences for concrete claims - applies unchanged to an insurance audience, with one addition specific to this sector: borrow the regulator's own words (evidence, outcomes, oversight, root cause) rather than reaching for adjectives, because those words are already the vocabulary this buyer is being measured in, and using them correctly is the fastest credibility signal available. Price stays an offer-stage detail, never the opening line, and no competitor is named - differentiate against the status quo of manual sampling, which m17 shows is still the honest majority position for roughly half of this market.

One structural point that applies to every kind of buyer here: the coverage claim ('every call we ingest, not a sample') is the headline statistic for a prospect who does not yet have full coverage, and it is the wrong opening for one that already does. ## Where this buyer actually is

There is a split in this market that matters for where the campaign agent looks. The **claims-side** buyer - claims director, claims operations manager, complaints manager - lives in insurance media and insurance events: Insurance Times, the MGAA calendar, BIBA, the claims conferences. The **quality-side** buyer - the QA manager, the person who actually runs the scorecard - lives in contact-centre media: Call Centre Helper, ContactBabel's research, the CX awards circuit. They are often in the same firm and rarely in the same room. A campaign that only works one of those two channels will reach half the buying committee.

The second thing worth noting is that the regulator is itself a gathering place. The FCA's good-and-poor-practice series and the Ombudsman's data releases are read, forwarded and discussed by exactly this audience, and they are free, dated and quotable. The FOS's own written evidence to the House of Lords inquiry is the single densest piece of insight about UK insurance complaints published this year and almost nobody in a vendor marketing team has read it.

The listed entries below are venues and publications, not people. Where a person is named anywhere in this pack they are the author or subject of a source, never a target.

## Answering honestly, not persuasively

Every objection below is answered only from live facts, or left open with the planned fact that admits the gap. Four patterns recur across all four kinds of buyer: security-review questions (SSO, hosting location, penetration testing), evidence-depth questions (a regulator-ready pack, listening to the call), telephony-fit questions, and 'why not what we already have' questions. The honest answer to the security and evidence-depth questions is frequently 'not today', and the discipline here is to say that plainly rather than talk around it - a buyer in a regulated sector will ask again at the security review if the first answer was vague, and will trust the rest of the pitch less for it.

claims.text: Where the honest answer to a live objection is that a capability is not yet available, the product's own boundary facts (all marked status: planned) are cited directly rather than answered around, and the objection is never promised a future date.

m12.body:
## What the rules actually permit on this card

Two channels are on the card, email and LinkedIn, and they are governed by different instruments with different consequences. Email is governed by PECR and the UK GDPR, enforced by the ICO. LinkedIn is governed by a contract with LinkedIn, enforced by account restriction. Neither bars this campaign, but each shapes it.

On email, the load-bearing distinction is the one PECR draws between corporate and individual subscribers. The ICO states plainly that the rule on marketing by electronic mail does not apply to corporate subscribers, so consent under PECR is not required to send a B2B marketing email to a corporate body. That is the permission this campaign runs on. Two caveats sit on top of it and both are the ICO's own words rather than an interpretation. First, sole traders and most partnerships are treated as individual subscribers, not corporate ones, which means consent or the soft opt-in applies to them; in this market that catches a small number of one-person MGA and consultancy shells rather than the target set, but the list build must not assume every FCA-registered entity is a corporate body. Second, a named work address is still personal data, so the UK GDPR applies in full: lawful basis, transparency, and an honoured right to object. The practical effect is that an opt-out must work on the first request, every time.

On LinkedIn there is no regulator, only the User Agreement. Section 8.2 prohibits using "bots or other automated methods to access the Services, add or download contacts, send or redirect messages", and LinkedIn's own help page states that third-party software or browser extensions that scrape, modify the appearance of, or automate activity on LinkedIn are a violation of the User Agreement and can result in account restriction. This does not bar LinkedIn outreach; it bars automating it. Manual connection requests and manually written messages from a real account are within the rules. The rule is a constraint on tooling, not on the channel.

One sector-specific point that is not a contact rule but behaves like one: the buyer is an FCA-regulated firm, and inbound approaches that look like a financial promotion attract a different kind of scrutiny. Nothing in a QA-software pitch is a financial promotion, but any claim about regulatory outcomes ("this makes you Consumer Duty compliant") is both false against the facts file and the kind of statement a compliance officer at the receiving end will forward internally. Keep the claim operational.

rules.rule: PECR's electronic mail marketing rule does not apply to corporate subscribers, so no PECR consent is needed to send a B2B marketing email to a corporate body such as an FCA-authorised insurer, MGA or TPA registered as a company. This is what makes cold email to this buyer set lawful under PECR.

Sole traders and (per the ICO's corporate/individual subscriber split) most partnerships are individual subscribers, so electronic mail marketing to them requires consent or the soft opt-in. Any list of small insurance intermediaries must therefore be screened for unincorporated entities before send.

Where the marketing uses personal data - which a named individual's work email address is - the UK GDPR applies alongside PECR, including lawfulness, fairness and transparency and the individual's right to object; an objection must be honoured and the contact removed.

The ICO's electronic mail marketing guidance also prohibits instigating forwarding ('forward to a friend' style referral marketing), because the instigator remains responsible for PECR compliance on the onward message. Do not build a referral mechanic into the email sequence.

LinkedIn's User Agreement, section 8.2 Dos and Don'ts, prohibits developing, supporting or using software, devices, scripts, robots or other means to scrape or copy the Services, and prohibits using bots or other unauthorised automated methods to access the Services, add or download contacts, or send or redirect messages. Manual outreach from a real account is permitted; automated connection or message sending is not.

LinkedIn's help centre states it does not allow third-party software or browser extensions that scrape, modify the appearance of, or automate activity on LinkedIn's website, describes this as a violation of the User Agreement, and restricts accounts found doing it until the software is disabled. The enforcement risk falls on the rep's own account.

LinkedIn reserves the right to limit how members connect and interact, including the number of connections and the ability to contact other members, and to restrict, suspend or terminate an account that breaches the Dos and Don'ts or the Professional Community Policies. Volume assumptions for LinkedIn outreach should therefore be treated as capped by the platform, not by the rep's time.

claims.text: The ICO states that the PECR rule on direct marketing by electronic mail does not apply to corporate subscribers, so B2B marketing emails may be sent to a corporate body without PECR consent, while the UK GDPR still applies whenever personal data is processed for direct marketing in a business context.
PECR reforms under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 raised the maximum fine from GBP 500,000 to GBP 17.5 million, which raises the cost of getting electronic marketing wrong.

## Dates that already exist

These are facts with dates, gathered so the campaign agent can decide what to do with them. Three kinds are mixed here deliberately, because they carry different weight. Regulatory dates (the FOS case fee, the Consumer Duty anniversary, the FCA's expanded workplan) are the ones that change a buyer's budget conversation. Data-publication dates (the FOS quarterly and half-yearly releases) are the ones that give a rep a reason to be in touch with a specific firm about a specific number. Event dates are where this buyer physically gathers, and two of them - the MGA Claims Conference on 5 November and The Claims Network: London on 17 November - are unusually well targeted at exactly the claims-operations population in the brief.

One caution the campaign agent should carry: the two November claims events are described by their organisers as senior, invitation-only gatherings whose named speakers are chief claims officers at large carriers and Lloyd's businesses. That audience skews above this brief's 250-seat band. They remain useful as a dated conversational hook and as a place the buyer's own bosses will be, not as a lead source inside the size filter.

## What the rep may say, verbatim, and what it must not become

Every line below rests on a live fact. Several carry a note because the fact file's own wording is binding - not stylistic advice but a boundary on what may honestly be claimed. The two most misuse-prone facts are the coverage claim and the security-audit claim: the first must never be inflated to a literal '100% of your calls' or applied to any call the pipeline did not ingest, and the second must never be upgraded from 'internally audited' to 'penetration tested' or an implication of a third party.

proof.note: Say 'every call we ingest', never 'every call you make' or a literal '100% of your calls'.
proof.text: Every call the pipeline ingests is transcribed and scored - not a sampled subset.
Every analysed call is scored against the customer's own QA rules, each with a weight and pass threshold, producing a score, a grade and a per-rule pass/fail list.

proof.note: Quote prices openly per brand voice; in cold outbound sequences, keep this to the offer stage, not the opening message.
proof.text: Three plans priced per seat per month with a pooled monthly allowance of analysed call hours: Starter GBP 4.99 with 40 hours, Professional GBP 7.99 with 70 hours, Enterprise GBP 9.99 with 100 hours.
There is no minimum number of seats and no annual commitment; plans are month to month.

proof.note: Coverage today is Settings writes only; never call it a full audit trail of every user action.
proof.text: Settings changes are written to an append-only audit log recording who changed what, when, from which IP, with before and after values.

proof.note: This was an internal audit. Say 'internally audited', never 'pen-tested'.
proof.text: Tenant data scoping across all API routes was internally audited on 12 July 2026 with no cross-tenant leaks found.

proof.note: Say 'Conversant is ISO 27001 certified'. Do not name the certification body or claim a scope beyond the group certificate.
proof.text: Conversant is ISO/IEC 27001 certified at group level, and Insights360 is developed and operated under that ISMS.

proof.note: Configurable risk types, not a purpose-built vulnerability-detection module - never claim automatic vulnerability detection.
proof.text: Calls are flagged against a list of risk types the customer defines, and flagged calls are listed on a Risks page and counted on the dashboard.

proof.note: Do not name any customer or quote a customer count; this general statement is as far as this fact may go.
proof.text: Insights360 is in production with paying customers using it day to day.

## Four findings, not a plan

Each kind of buyer in m03 carries at least four sourced pains, so each has a candidate below. They are ranked by how close the pain sits to a dated, checkable consequence - the outsourced claims handler first, because its client's own regulator obligation is already published and dated; the motor operation last, not because its pain is smaller, but because its complaint-volume trend is contested between two credible sources (see m17) and roughly half of this segment already reports full call coverage, which narrows the honest opening. The campaign agent decides sequencing, channel mix and volume; these are findings about which door to knock on and why, not an order to knock on them.

claims.text: Candidates are ranked by how directly and recently a dated regulatory or financial event attaches to the pain, not by estimated deal size; the outsourced-claims-handler and travel-desk pains both trace to FCA and Ombudsman publications inside the last twelve months, while the motor pain's trend is contested between two 2026 sources.

candidates.wrongIf: The TPA already publicly markets an FCA-aligned QA and audit-trail service to its own clients as fully solved (see m17's Sedgwick contradiction), or its telephony is an uncosted Avaya or Genesys scoping project the firm will not fund quickly.
candidates.leadAngle: Your clients have been told to evidence how they oversee the third parties handling their claims; hand them a call-level record instead of a sample.

candidates.whyNow: The Financial Ombudsman's Q1 2026/27 data, published 22 July 2026, shows travel complaints up 30% year on year, inside the FCA's expanded home-and-travel claims review.
candidates.wrongIf: The desk's UK claims and assistance headcount sits inside a group whose worldwide total is far above 250 seats and the UK desk itself cannot be confirmed as inside the band, or the firm already runs AI reviewing every call.

m17.body:
## What argues against this pack

Six findings cut against the campaign as this pack has framed it. Two of them are serious enough to change how the messaging is built, and the campaign agent should read them before anything else in this module.

The first is that **the regulatory paperwork burden is going down, not up**. This pack's urgency rests on an evidential standard, and in June and July 2026 the FCA published CP26/22 and CP26/23 proposing to simplify insurance rules and clarify Consumer Duty scope and proportionality - and confirmed that firms do not need to produce a standalone Consumer Duty board report. An outreach line built on "your board report needs outcomes evidence" can be answered in one sentence by any compliance officer who has read the consultations. The durable urgency is the Ombudsman case fee and the FCA's *supervisory* work on claims handling, both of which continue regardless.

The second is that **coverage has already been bought by about half of this market**. MaxContact's research puts AI reviewing every call at 46.7% against manual sampling at 49.5% among 285 FCA-regulated contact centres. The reference worked example this brand uses - the 30-seat broker whose 7,600 calls go unreviewed - is still true of the other half, but it is no longer a surprise to anyone. Expect "we already have that" as the most common first reply, and expect it to be true about as often as not.

The rest are smaller but real. Motor complaint volumes fell through 2025 on the annual measure even as they rose on the latest quarterly one, so the trend statement depends entirely on which dataset is quoted - quote both or quote the one that is dated most recently and say so. Large TPAs market FCA-aligned QA, audit trails and MI reporting as already embedded in their service, which removes the buying reason for their insurer clients and, if true of a given TPA, removes it for the TPA too. Practitioners and vendors alike report that agents distrust machine scoring and that AI QA projects fail when nobody owns the insights - a failure mode this product is exposed to, because the facts file confirms there is no reviewer workflow, no assignment and no SLA tracking on the needs-review list. And the FCA declined to launch a market study in response to the Which? super-complaint, and rejected part of Which?'s legal analysis, which tempers the "the regulator is coming" framing.

claims.text: The FCA published CP26/22 (Simplifying the Insurance Rules) on 29 June 2026, closing 4 September 2026, and CP26/23 (Consumer Duty: Scope and Proportionality), closing 18 September 2026; the proposals are deregulatory in nature and firms are not required to change their approach where it already meets existing standards.

a.text: Clifford Chance reports that the FCA has confirmed firms do not need to produce a standalone Consumer Duty board report, and that reporting should instead be proportionate to the firm's role and activities, with governance frameworks having become unnecessarily complex at many firms.

entries.text: The pack's Consumer Duty board-report urgency is undercut by the FCA's own 2026 simplification programme: firms do not need to produce a standalone Consumer Duty board report, and reporting should be proportionate to the firm's role and activities. Any messaging built on an annual board report obligation must be rewritten around supervisory claims-handling work and case-fee cost instead.
entries.meaning: Drop 'your board report needs evidence' as a lead angle. Keep 'the FCA is reviewing claims handling and third-party oversight' and 'a referred case costs GBP 680' - both survive the simplification programme.

a.text: Among 285 FCA-regulated UK contact centres surveyed, 46.7% already have AI reviewing every single call while 49.5% still use manual sampling - the research's own conclusion is that coverage is no longer the constraint.

b.text: Call Centre Helper's research reports the industry standard as random scoring of four advisor calls per month, with 41% of contact centres monitoring fewer than four calls per advisor per month, and its community discussion in 2026 still centres on how many calls to sample by hand.

entries.text: Two credible sources disagree about whether call-review coverage is still an open problem in FCA-regulated contact centres: one puts AI reviewing every call at 46.7% and manual sampling at 49.5%, while the contact-centre standard reported elsewhere is four calls per agent per month with 41% of centres monitoring fewer than four.
entries.meaning: Both can be true - the market has split. The campaign must qualify early whether the prospect already runs automated scoring, because for roughly half of them the coverage pitch is answering a solved problem, and for the other half it is the whole argument. Treat the answer as a routing question, not as an objection.

a.text: Insurance DataLab's analysis found 12,860 motor-related FOS complaints in 2025, a year-on-year drop of 15.5% against 2024, with the uphold rate improving from 43% to 36.5% and volumes having fallen in five of the last six quarters.

b.text: The Financial Ombudsman's Q1 2026/27 release, published 22 July 2026, reports car or motorcycle insurance complaints rising to 4,100 from 2,800 in the same period of 2025.

entries.text: The direction of motor insurance complaints depends on which dataset is quoted: annual FOS data analysed in March 2026 shows motor complaints down 15.5% year on year with uphold rates improving, while the FOS's own July 2026 quarterly release shows car and motorcycle complaints up from 2,800 to 4,100 year on year.
entries.meaning: Do not build a motor angle on 'complaints are rising' without naming the quarter and the source. The safest formulation is the Q1 2026/27 quarterly figure with its date attached; a prospect who has read the annual analysis will otherwise correct the claim and lose trust in everything else in the email.

a.text: Sedgwick's UK international TPA services page states that its TPA model embeds FCA-aligned standards, quality assurance, audit trails, MI reporting and governance frameworks into every programme, removing the need for additional internal oversight.

entries.text: Large TPAs market FCA-aligned quality assurance, audit trails, MI reporting and governance as embedded in their service - explicitly framed as removing the need for additional internal oversight by the insurer. If a target TPA already sells that story to its clients, the outsourced-claims-handler pain as framed in this pack is one they publicly claim to have solved.
entries.meaning: For the outsourced-claims-handler kind of buyer, open on what the client's oversight team asks for in evidence, not on whether the TPA has a quality framework. Assume they have a framework and probe what it is built from - a sample, or every call.

a.text: Industry commentary reports that agents are sceptical of being scored by a machine and that trust must be built through transparency and supportive coaching, and separately that platforms generating insights without an owner for those insights produce dashboards nobody checks - an organisational design gap technology cannot fix.
a.inferredFrom: provenance: fewer than two of its distinctive words on the page (separately, commentary, nobody)

entries.text: Two failure modes are widely reported for automated QA: agents distrust being scored by a machine, and analytics projects produce dashboards nobody checks when no one owns acting on the insight. The second is a live risk for this product specifically, because the facts file records that the needs-review list is a list and not a workflow - no assignment to reviewers, no status, no SLA tracking.
entries.meaning: Do not promise an outcome that depends on a workflow that does not ship. The honest framing is that the scoring and the flagging are automatic and the acting on them remains the team's job - and that this should be said out loud, because the buyer will discover it in week two otherwise.

a.text: The FCA decided not to launch a market study or revise consumer protection rules following the Which? super-complaint, rejected Which?'s conclusion on the sample of policy documents, and noted that 79% of consumers who make an insurance claim are satisfied with how it was handled, while 3 in 10 said there is not enough information to judge the quality of different policies.

entries.text: The FCA did not launch a market study or revise consumer protection rules in response to the Which? super-complaint, rejected Which?'s conclusion that a sample of policy documents evidenced unfair application of contract terms, and stated it had not failed its statutory consumer protection objective - it chose supervisory tools instead.
entries.meaning: The regulator is acting, but it is not escalating in the way an alarmist message would imply, and it publicly said 79% of consumers who make an insurance claim are satisfied with how it was handled. Keep the regulatory reference factual and narrow: expanded reviews of claims handling and third-party oversight, two enforcement cases opened, one firm stopped from growing. Do not extrapolate.

repSummary.body: Five lines for the rep, in plain words.
lines: Reach claims ops, QA and complaints leads at mid-sized GB insurers, MGAs, claims handlers and brokers running 5-250 seat claims teams - not the huge insurers, and not the people answering the phones.
The FCA is actively reviewing how insurers handle claims and oversee outsourced claims teams, and from April 2026 every case that reaches the Ombudsman costs the firm GBP 680.
Open with what the FCA is doing and the new case fee before anything about the product - most claims teams still only check four to eight calls per handler each month.

About half of these firms already review every call some other way, so the biggest unknown is which half you're talking to - ask early, and if they already have it, talk about speed and proof instead of coverage.

Twenty firms this size carry real complaint volume across motor, travel, home and delegated claims in Great Britain, priced with no seat minimum and no annual contract - worth a focused three-week push by email and LinkedIn.

execSummary.icp: A GB-headquartered general insurance carrier, MGA, TPA or outsourced claims handler, or mid-tier broker/consolidator with an in-house claims or complaints contact centre of 5 to 250 seats. Buying committee of 2-4: a claims operations, QA or complaints lead as champion or signer, a compliance or conduct-risk officer as co-champion, and at the smallest firms an MD or COO who is both. execSummary.body:
## The one page

UK general insurance claims and complaints telephone operations of 5-250 seats sit inside a live FCA review of claims handling and third-party oversight and a new GBP 680 Ombudsman case fee, and most still run QA on a four-to-eight-call-per-agent-per-month human sample. Insights360 scores every call the pipeline ingests against the buyer's own rules, at a price with no seat minimum and no annual commitment, which is what makes coverage reachable below the size where enterprise QA tools are viable. The honest complication is that roughly half of FCA-regulated contact centres already report AI reviewing every call, so the pitch has to qualify early and split: coverage for the half that lacks it, latency and provability of evidence for the half that has it. Four kinds of buyer carry this pain with different urgency and different economics, from the fastest-closing delegated-authority MGA to the highest-volume specialist motor operation, and none of them should be sold the three things this product does not yet do: a regulator-ready evidence pack, in-app audio playback, or a view across more than one entity.

claims.text: The FCA's 18 December 2025 response to the Which? super-complaint expanded its insurance workplan to review firms' claims-handling customer service and delivery and how firms oversee third parties that handle claims, disclosing 2 enforcement cases opened, 1 firm stopped from growing its business, 3 independent reviews into firms' systems and controls, and 3 senior managers made to agree fixes.
From 1 April 2026 respondent firms are charged GBP 680 per Financial Ombudsman case, with the previous three-free-cases arrangement replaced by a GBP 2,000 annual allowance.
Research with 285 FCA-regulated UK contact centre managers and directors found manual sampling and AI reviewing every call running almost neck and neck, at 49.5% and 46.7% respectively.

execSummary.verdict: Proceed, with the coverage pitch qualified rather than led: open on the FCA's named review of claims handling and third-party oversight and the GBP 680 case fee, ask early whether the prospect already has AI reviewing every call, and route accordingly - coverage for the half that lacks it, latency and provability of evidence for the half that has it. Never let the pitch drift into the compliance-evidence-pack, audio-playback, cross-tenant or security-surface features it does not yet ship, and never name a competitor.
productConstraints: No regulator-ready compliance evidence packs (planned, not shipped) - never position as satisfying an FCA review directly.
No in-app audio playback - 'listen to the evidence' cannot be promised.
No group or cross-tenant dashboard - each entity sees only its own tenant.
No SSO, SCIM, PII or card-number redaction, or CRM connectors - a security review will surface this.
Hosting is EU (Frankfurt, Germany), not the UK.
Results land within roughly an hour, not in real time and never 'within minutes'.
Only 3CX, OAK/ClarifyGo and RingCentral have an automated telephony feed; Avaya, Teams and Genesys-class estates common in insurance are scoped per customer.
The needs-review list has no assignment, status or SLA workflow.
execSummary.competitivePosition: Against UK-facing conduct-risk specialists (MaxContact, Aveni, Voyc) already selling the same regulatory story, and against mid-market auto-QA platforms (EvaluAgent from USD 35/seat, Scorebuddy quote-only) that outsell Insights360 on security surface it does not yet have (SSO, PII redaction, in-app playback), Insights360's durable edge is price accessible below a QA function's economic floor, no seat minimum and no annual lock-in - not a features race it can currently win. Manual sampling remains a credible do-nothing option, and roughly half of FCA-regulated contact centres already report full call coverage, so coverage alone is not a universal differentiator.
